title: Threat2Traffic: Multi-Agent Environment Synthesis for Malware Traffic Generation from Threat Intelligence
one_liner: The paper turns threat reports into executable malware environments by extracting the exact conditions a sample needs, building those conditions automatically, and validating the result before running the malware.
lead: Malware traffic data is valuable because defenders need realistic examples of command-and-control messages, downloads, and beacon patterns to train detectors. Real malware traffic is hard to collect at scale. Old public datasets are outdated, and generic sandboxes often fail because many malware samples activate only when specific services, files, credentials, domains, or timing conditions are present. Threat2Traffic treats threat-intelligence reports as a source of those missing requirements. It uses several language-model agents to read evidence, infer what the malware needs, synthesize a tailored environment, and check that the resulting setup is internally consistent before executing the sample.

problem.h2: Why malware does not reveal itself in a generic sandbox
paras: A malware sample does not produce useful traffic merely because it is executed. Many samples check their environment first. They may need a reachable command server, a specific operating-system service, a registry key, a mutex name, an installed application, or a realistic user context. If those conditions are absent, the sample may stay quiet, terminate, or follow a harmless branch. A one-size-fits-all sandbox misses this sample-specific setup.

Human analysts often reconstruct these dependencies by reading reverse-engineering notes or threat reports and then hand-building a custom environment. That process is slow and hard to scale. The technical challenge is not only extracting facts from prose. The system must separate direct evidence from speculation, resolve contradictions across sources, and turn text descriptions into concrete environment objects that can actually be deployed.

callout.html: You do not get realistic malware traffic unless the execution environment satisfies the sample's own preconditions.

panels.title: 1. Threat report arrives
panels.caption: The information about what the malware needs is scattered across unstructured threat intelligence.

panels.title: 2. Agents extract evidence
panels.caption: Different agents propose and challenge candidate dependencies so the system does not accept one reading too quickly.

panels.title: 3. Build an evidence graph
panels.viz_args: dependency claims linked to supporting text and constraints
panels.caption: Each required artifact is attached to evidence, confidence, and compatibility checks.

panels.title: 4. Synthesize the environment
panels.viz_args: services, files, domains, credentials, timing conditions
panels.caption: The system turns the extracted requirements into a machine-executable environment specification.

panels.title: 5. Run and capture traffic
panels.caption: After validation, the malware is executed in the tailored environment and its traffic is recorded.

steps.text: Parse reports, notes, and indicators into candidate dependency statements because the raw text itself cannot be executed.
Let several agents propose, challenge, and reconcile dependency claims so that ambiguous phrasing is less likely to become a mistaken environment requirement.
Store each dependency with its supporting passages and relations to other dependencies, which means later synthesis can reason about consistency instead of relying on one flat list.
Generate configuration artifacts such as hosts, services, files, and network conditions that satisfy the extracted requirements.
Check both syntax and semantics so the generated environment is not only well-formed but also compatible with the malware's expected behavior.

paras: The paper changes the way malware-analysis environments are created. Instead of launching every sample inside the same generic sandbox, it builds one environment per sample from documented behavioral requirements.
object.object: the mapping from threat intelligence to executable sandbox configuration

hidden.name: the minimal set of environmental dependencies that trigger malicious behavior
paras: The main quantity is not the entire content of the threat report. It is the subset of conditions that the malware actually checks or relies on before revealing its network behavior. Some details in a report are descriptive background. Others are operational preconditions. The system must recover the second group.

Threat2Traffic represents this quantity with an evidence graph so that each dependency claim has provenance and relations to other claims. That structure matters because environment synthesis must know not only that a domain or service is mentioned, but also whether it is mandatory, optional, or conditional on another artifact.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark claims that directly determine whether the malware will enter the behavior path that emits useful traffic.

reads.html: The method is trying to recover the exact setup the malware needs before it starts acting maliciously on the network.
The framework extracts sample-specific behavioral dependencies from threat intelligence and organizes them as evidence-backed constraints for environment synthesis.

mechanism.h2: Why the multi-agent evidence-to-environment pipeline works
paras: The pipeline helps because the task has two separate failure modes. The first is reading failure: threat reports are incomplete, noisy, and ambiguous, so a single pass can confuse observed behavior with required preconditions. Multi-agent deliberation reduces that risk because one agent can propose a dependency while another checks whether the supporting text actually justifies it. The evidence graph then preserves those justifications so later stages can inspect them.

The second failure mode is synthesis failure. Even a correct list of dependencies is not enough unless it can be turned into a runnable environment. Invariant-guided synthesis helps because it constrains generation with rules the environment must satisfy, such as valid host relationships, reachable services, or compatibility between configuration choices. Dual-layer validation matters because a generated file may be syntactically correct but behaviorally useless. The semantic validation step asks whether the combined environment is likely to satisfy the malware's real execution path.

stages.s: tailored sandbox that yields malware traffic

math.h2: Choose the environment that satisfies the most evidence-backed constraints
math.words: Score a candidate environment by how many required dependencies it satisfies minus penalties for unsupported or inconsistent configuration choices.
math.equation: score(E) = sum_i w_i * satisfy(E, d_i) - lambda * inconsistency(E)
symbols: the importance or confidence weight for dependency d_i
an indicator that the environment fulfills that dependency
a penalty for conflicting or invalid configuration choices
the quantity the synthesis process tries to maximize

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the malware needs one reachable domain, one registry key, and one running service.
Candidate environment A satisfies all three but adds one conflicting network rule.
Candidate environment B satisfies only the domain and registry key, with no conflicts.
If all three dependencies have weight 1 and the conflict penalty weight is 1, A gets 3 minus 1, which is 2.
B gets 2 minus 0, which is also 2.
A later semantic check can then break the tie by preferring the environment whose full behavior path is more plausible.

math.note: The exact implementation is more elaborate than this toy score, but the logic is the same: synthesis should reward satisfying supported dependencies and punish contradictions.

charts.title: Generic or manually limited baselines
charts.note: A generic sandbox misses many behavior-trigger conditions, so samples often fail to expose the traffic patterns analysts need even though the malware technically executes.

charts.title: Threat2Traffic
charts.note: The paper reports 83.1 percent reproduction success across 1,077 samples because the system builds the environment around each sample's own documented requirements instead of forcing all samples through one default setup.

items.b: Threat reports may omit a required dependency.
items.html: If the source documents never mention a required file, service, or timing condition, the system cannot synthesize it from evidence alone, so the malware may still remain dormant.

items.b: Evidence graph errors can cascade into synthesis.
items.html: A mistaken claim that survives deliberation can become a hard environment constraint, which means the synthesis stage may faithfully build the wrong world.

items.b: Semantic validation is still a proxy.
items.html: A generated environment can pass structural checks and still fail to trigger the intended malware branch because real malicious behavior may depend on factors the proxy validator does not observe.

The method works when threat intelligence contains enough operational detail and the validation stage catches contradictions, because then the synthesized environment is close enough to the malware's expected setting to trigger its network behavior.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a contained toy version with benign samples that activate only when specific environment conditions are met, such as a reachable domain, a local file, and a named service. Write short threat-style reports that describe those dependencies with some ambiguity. Then compare a generic sandbox, a single-agent extractor, and the full multi-agent evidence-graph pipeline.

The demo should show two things separately: extraction quality and traffic yield. That split matters because a system can produce plausible dependency lists while still failing to synthesize a runnable environment.
demo.closing: A convincing result shows that more samples reveal their network behavior only after the environment is tailored from evidence-backed dependencies.
